etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ymaginacioun, from Old French imaginacion, ymaginacion, from Latin imāginātiō.

definitions.definition: The image-making power of the mind; the act of mentally creating or reproducing an object not previously perceived; the ability to create such images.

quote.citation: 1913, Robert Barr, chapter 5, in Lord Stranleigh Abroad‎[1]:
quote.text: She removed Stranleigh’s coat with a dexterity that aroused his imagination.

definitions.definition: Particularly, construction of false images; fantasizing.
A mental image formed by the action of the imagination as a faculty; something imagined.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Youth and Age”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC:
quote.text: And yet the invention of young men, is more lively than that of old; and imaginations stream into their minds better, and, as it were, more divinely.
